cards.title: The tunnel to nowhere
cards.text: A miner named William "Burro" Schmidt dug a tunnel through the El Paso Mountains with a pick, a shovel, a four-pound hammer, and carefully placed dynamite. He began in 1906, and by 1938 he had reached his goal. Schmidt said he would never haul his ore to the Mojave smelter down the back trail with his two burros. A road from Last Chance Canyon to Mojave was completed in 1920, but he kept digging. He never used the tunnel to carry ore.

cards.title: A landing field becomes a weapons laboratory
cards.text: China Lake began as an emergency landing field that the Works Progress Administration built in the early 1930s near the town of Inyokern. The field opened in 1935, and the Army Air Forces acquired it in 1942. In November 1943, it was transferred to the Navy, which made it the Naval Ordnance Test Station. The desert around it is vast and sparsely populated, with near-perfect flying weather and practically unlimited visibility.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: Bigger than Rhode Island
cards.text: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake covers more than 1.1 million acres, an area larger than the state of Rhode Island. It is the Navy's largest single landholding. The part of the base inside Kern County is about 1.4 percent of the county, as of 2024.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: Five inches of rain
cards.text: At China Lake, in eastern Kern County, only about 4.7 inches of rain falls in an average year. The average temperature over the year is about 65 degrees. July afternoons average a high near 105 degrees. January nights average a low of about 31 degrees.

cards.title: What the county government does with its money
cards.text: Kern County's government spent about 2.6 billion dollars in 2022. It had about 10,000 full-time employees that year. Property taxes brought in about 423 million dollars of its tax revenue. An elected board of five supervisors, serving four-year terms, governs the county.

cards.title: A base of 470 square miles
cards.text: Edwards Air Force Base covers 301,000 acres, about 470 square miles. More than 120 million dollars was spent to develop and expand it in the 1940s. About 4 percent of Kern County lies inside the base, as of 2024.

cards.title: Breaking the sound barrier
cards.text: On October 14, 1947, over what is now Edwards Air Force Base, Captain Chuck Yeager became the first person to fly faster than the speed of sound. He flew a Bell XS-1 nicknamed Glamorous Glennis, and a sonic boom was heard across the Mojave Desert. The flight was over Rogers Dry Lake, a dry lakebed so flat that it could serve as a giant runway. Back then the base was called Muroc, a reversal of Corum, because California already had a town named Coram. It was later renamed for Captain Glen Edwards, who died in 1948 in the crash of a Northrop YB-49 flying wing.

cards.title: A mining town was the first county seat
cards.text: Kern County's first county seat was Havilah, a mining town, not Bakersfield. The county was created in 1866 from southern Tulare County, with added land from Los Angeles and San Bernardino Counties. The seat moved to Bakersfield in 1874.

cards.title: Pistachios in a dry valley
cards.text: A company that grows pistachios in the Indian Wells Valley went to court over a fee for pumping the valley's groundwater. The local groundwater authority set a replenishment fee of 2,130 dollars an acre-foot, starting in January 2021. The grower, Mojave Pistachios, argued the fee infringed on its water rights. In February 2024, the California Court of Appeals ruled in the authority's favor.

cards.title: One basin, no backup
cards.text: The towns around Ridgecrest and the China Lake base draw their water from one underground basin, with no significant surface water or imported supply. The state has determined that the Indian Wells Valley groundwater basin is in critical overdraft, from decades of over-pumping. The basin spans about 600 square miles across parts of Kern, Inyo, and San Bernardino Counties. Groundwater levels there have been declining since 1945. State law requires pumping and recharge to be brought into balance by 2040.

cards.title: Two towns moved for the lake
cards.text: To make room for the Isabella Dam reservoir, the towns of Lake Isabella and Kernville both had to be moved to higher ground. Most of the original town of Kernville had been razed in 1948. Construction began in 1948 and finished in March 1953. Lake Isabella can hold up to 570,000 acre-feet of water, with a surface area of 11,200 acres.

cards.title: Raising a dam sixteen feet
cards.text: The Army Corps of Engineers raised both the main and auxiliary dams at Lake Isabella by 16 feet. A seepage problem was found in the auxiliary dam on April 28, 2006, and the lake was held 20 feet below its normal full level. The work also added a new 28-foot-high labyrinth weir, and it targeted three failure risks: overtopping, seepage, and earthquake damage. The safety improvements were substantially completed in November 2022.

cards.title: The Kawaiisu homeland
cards.text: The Kawaiisu live in the Tehachapi Valley and north across Tehachapi Pass, toward Lake Isabella and Walker Pass. They call themselves Nüwa, which means the People. Before European contact, they lived in permanent winter villages of 60 to 100 people. They also traveled east on food-gathering trips into the northern Mojave Desert, as far as the Panamint Valley. The Kawaiisu once made their home around what is now Red Rock Canyon State Park, and they left petroglyphs in the El Paso Mountains.

cards.title: Oil at seventy feet
cards.text: In 1899, Tom Means persuaded Frank Wiseman and others to dig for oil in what became the Kern River Oil Field, and they found it at 70 feet. Kern County's economy is still heavily linked to agriculture and petroleum extraction.

cards.title: A preserve on an old cattle ranch
cards.text: The Kern River Preserve, near Weldon, is owned by the National Audubon Society. It covers about 3,000 acres on the former cattle ranch of Andrew Brown, which dates to the 1860s. The preserve was established in 1979. The South Fork Kern River, which flows through it into Lake Isabella, has been a national Wild and Scenic River since 1987. The preserve protects habitat for the federally listed endangered southwestern willow flycatcher.

cards.title: Who owns the land
cards.text: Government agencies and conservation groups manage about a third of Kern County, as of 2024. The Bureau of Land Management has the biggest share, about 14 percent of the county, and its Ridgecrest Field Office alone covers nearly 10 percent. The Forest Service manages about 7 percent, most of it Sequoia National Forest. The Defense Department holds about 5.5 percent, nearly all of it Edwards Air Force Base and China Lake.

cards.title: From county airfield to airliner parking lot
cards.text: Kern County opened the Mojave Airport in 1935. After the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the Marine Corps took it over and expanded it into a Marine Corps Auxiliary Air Station. Today the airport is also known as a place where commercial airliners are stored, because of the vast area and dry desert conditions.

cards.title: Where the twenty-mule teams stopped
cards.text: Mojave was the western end of the twenty-mule-team borax route from Death Valley. In the 1880s, teams hauled borax about 165 miles from Death Valley to the railroad at Mojave. The town began in 1876 as a construction camp on the Southern Pacific Railroad. It later served as headquarters for construction of the Los Angeles Aqueduct.

cards.title: The first private spaceflight
cards.text: Mojave Air and Space Port was the base of the first privately funded human spaceflight, SpaceShipOne's flight on June 21, 2004. SpaceShipOne went on to win the X Prize with flights on September 29 and October 4, 2004.

cards.title: A county named for a mapmaker
cards.text: Kern County is named for the Kern River, and the river is named for a mapmaker. Edward Kern was the cartographer on John Frémont's 1845 expedition, which crossed Walker Pass. In 1776, a Spanish priest, Father Francisco Garcés, had called the same river the Rio Bravo de San Felipe.

cards.title: Who lives here
cards.text: About 915,000 people live in Kern County, as of 2024, spread across about 8,135 square miles of land. Half of its residents are younger than about 33. The median household income was about 70,200 dollars a year. The median home was worth about 338,000 dollars.

cards.title: A gold camp that grew up overnight
cards.text: In April 1895, Frederic Mooers, John Singleton, and Charles Burcham found gold at the Yellow Aster Mine, and a camp that became Randsburg grew around it. The mine and camp were named for the Rand, the gold mining region of South Africa. By the end of 1896, more than 1,500 people lived in the camp. As of 2020, Randsburg had 45 residents.

cards.title: Cliffs striped red and white
cards.text: The cliffs of Red Rock Canyon State Park get their vivid colors from alternating layers of white clay and red sandstone. The park covers about 27,000 acres along Highway 14, about 25 miles northeast of Mojave. In the early 1870s, its colorful formations served as landmarks for twenty-mule-team freight wagons. The area was once home to the Kawaiisu people. The state park was created in 1968.

cards.title: A desert backlot
cards.text: Movies shot at Red Rock Canyon State Park include Jurassic Park, Beneath the Planet of the Apes, and Westworld. Television series filmed there include Airwolf and Lost in Space.

cards.title: The Ridgecrest earthquakes
cards.text: The 2019 Ridgecrest earthquakes began with a magnitude 6.4 shock on July 4 and a magnitude 7.1 the next evening. More than 1,400 earthquakes were recorded by the evening of July 5, and more than 3,000 by the morning of July 7. The shaking was felt as far north as Sacramento, as far east as Phoenix, and as far south as Baja California. One person died and 25 were injured.

cards.title: The base that stopped
cards.text: After the July 2019 earthquakes, China Lake evacuated all nonessential personnel and was declared not mission capable. Aerial photographs showed a lateral offset of three to five feet on a service road. The Navy's damage assessment totaled about 5.2 billion dollars. Replacing the buildings alone would cost about 2.2 billion dollars.

cards.title: A missile from the Mojave
cards.text: The Sidewinder air-to-air missile came out of China Lake, then called the Naval Ordnance Test Station. Scientists and engineers there developed the AIM-9 version of the Sidewinder in 1950. William McLean led the project team developing it from 1945 to 1954. Its variants and upgrades are still in active service.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: People of the upper Kern River
cards.text: The Tübatulabal are an Indigenous people of the upper Kern River valley, in the southern Sierra Nevada. Their name loosely translates as pine-nut eaters, from a word for people who go to the forest to gather piñon nuts. Acorns and piñon nuts were staples of their diet, with fish second in importance. They had three bands, speaking mutually intelligible dialects of a Uto-Aztecan language. A Tübatulabal tribe, with an office in Mountain Mesa, has been seeking federal recognition.

cards.title: Around the world without stopping
cards.text: The Rutan Voyager, the first aircraft to fly around the world nonstop and unrefueled, was built in Mojave. Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew it in December 1986.

cards.title: A pass that has barely changed
cards.text: Apart from the paved road, Walker Pass is essentially unaltered since Joseph R. Walker mapped it in 1834. John Frémont's survey expedition used the pass in 1845, and Frémont suggested it be named for Walker. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses there.

cards.title: A volcano split in two
cards.text: A volcano that erupted about 23 million years ago near present-day Lancaster was cut in half by the San Andreas Fault. One half stayed in the Antelope Valley area as the Neenach Formation. The other half is now Pinnacles National Park, {distance} {direction} of here.

cards.title: A valley floor that is sinking
cards.text: In the Antelope Valley, long-term pumping of groundwater has lowered the water table. That has made wells harder to pump, cut their efficiency, and caused the land surface to sink.

cards.title: Boiling mud and a power plant
cards.text: The Coso volcanic field is known for boiling mud pots and fumaroles within an area of many little-eroded volcanoes. Geothermal power began there in 1987, and the field now produces more than 270 megawatts of electricity. Since 1987 it has delivered more than 26,000 gigawatt-hours of electricity. Hot fluids are brought up from the fractured rock below, turned to steam to drive a turbine, and then reinjected into the ground.

cards.title: Obsidian for stone tools
cards.text: Obsidian from the Coso Volcanic Field was heavily exploited by the Native American Coso People between about 3,000 and 1,000 years ago. Geochemists have identified four subsources of the glass, including one at Sugarloaf and one at Joshua Ridge.

cards.title: A volcano field in a step-over
cards.text: The Coso Volcanic Field lies east of the Sierra Nevada, between Owens Valley and the Garlock Fault, in the Basin and Range province. It sits in a releasing step-over between the Little Lake fault and the Owens Valley fault, both active right-lateral strike-slip faults. Mesozoic plutonic and metamorphic rocks like those of the southern Sierra Nevada underlie the area, and the hot fluids are trapped in these fractured rocks.

cards.title: Thirty-eight rhyolite domes
cards.text: Volcanism began in the Coso Range about 6 million years ago. The region is best known for 38 high-silica rhyolite domes and lava flows that erupted in the Pleistocene, between about 1.1 million and 40,000 years ago, along with 14 basaltic centers. The domes form an elongate array atop a north-trending horst about 8 by 20 kilometers. The field's last listed eruption was about 39,000 years ago, though small episodes of ash emission and cone building may be Holocene in age.

cards.title: Lava that is older than it looks
cards.text: The Black Mountain Basalt in the El Paso Mountains was once thought to be Pleistocene in age, but it was shown to be Miocene. Four potassium-argon ages range from 15.1 to 17.9 million years. The basalt erupted mostly from east-west fissures, which reflects north-south extension between the Mojave Desert block and the southwestern Basin and Range. It is chemically distinctive, a potassium-poor high-alumina basalt.

cards.title: A mountain range on a fault block
cards.text: The El Paso Mountains are a typical fault block, pushed upward by strain just north of the Garlock Fault. The El Paso Fault, a branch of the Garlock, formed in response to the tearing caused by the Garlock Fault, and it trends northeast. The present topography began to form about 18 million years ago, when movement started on the Garlock Fault and its splays. Most of the uplifted rock has since been eroded away, leaving tilted layers with younger rock atop older rock in the canyon walls.

cards.title: Sediments from an ancient sea
cards.text: The Goler Formation is the oldest of the Cenozoic rock units in the El Paso Mountains, laid down between about 55 and 65 million years ago. A basin subsided here during the Paleocene and Eocene, and the formation holds as much as 13,050 feet of continental sediments in places. Near the top of the formation is fossiliferous mudstone, laid down when the sea reached this basin in a marine incursion. The formation was later tilted northward and eroded nearly flat before the Miocene.

cards.title: Why the cliffs are red and white
cards.text: The Ricardo Group, which gives the El Paso Mountains their famous red sandstone beds, is nearly 7,000 feet of coarse volcanic ash, lava flows, sandstones, lake-deposited silts and clays, and sandy gravels. Much of its red and pink color comes from the oxidation of iron-bearing minerals, and its white layers are mostly volcanic ash. Rain that runs over the exposed layers erodes the softer beds and leaves the effect of fluted columns. Because many of the deposits are volcanic ash or interlayered with lava flows, geologists can date them with good precision.

cards.title: A record of the Sierra Nevada rising
cards.text: Granitic gravels in the upper Ricardo Formation of the El Paso Mountains were shed eastward from the southern Sierra Nevada, beginning about 8 million years ago. They match the age of the Kern River Formation on the west side of the Sierra Nevada. They point to uplift of the Sierra Nevada along its eastern frontal fault.

cards.title: A lake that is usually dry
cards.text: Koehn Lake in the Fremont Valley is a dry lake that is closed to outflow in some seasons. Any water that collects there leaves by evaporation. The dry lakebed is about 5 miles long and 3 miles across at its widest. The Garlock Fault steps sideways across a gap about 3 kilometers wide near the lake.

cards.title: A shoreline the fault has moved
cards.text: Near Koehn Lake, a bar left by an ancient lake has been shifted sideways by the Garlock Fault. The bar is between 11,000 and 15,000 years old. Measuring how far it moved gave a slip rate of between 4 and 7 millimeters a year.

cards.title: Land set aside for the desert tortoise
cards.text: The Desert Tortoise Research Natural Area covers 39.5 square miles of the western Mojave Desert. It was set aside to protect the desert tortoise, which is California's state reptile. In 1980, the Bureau of Land Management designated it an Area of Critical Environmental Concern and a Research Natural Area. The area is fenced, and an interpretive center there was dedicated in April 1980.

cards.title: Earthquakes recorded in the ground
cards.text: Geologists dug a trench across the Garlock Fault south of the El Paso Mountains. Buried fissures and fault scarps there record five to eight surface-rupturing earthquakes in the past 5,000 years. A deeper dig later confirmed that the timing between earthquakes was irregular.

cards.title: The line between two landscapes
cards.text: The Garlock Fault separates the Tehachapi Mountains, the southern Sierra Nevada, and the Basin and Range country on its north side from the Mojave Desert on its south side. It runs from a junction with the San Andreas Fault in the west to the Avawatz Mountains near the south end of Death Valley. Rocks on the two sides have been slid sideways past each other by a maximum of 48 to 64 kilometers.

cards.title: Where the 2019 earthquake stopped
cards.text: The rupture of the 2019 Ridgecrest earthquake ended near the Garlock Fault. The Garlock Fault west of the rupture's end was unclamped, meaning the force pressing its two sides together had eased. Soon afterward, the Garlock Fault began slowly creeping, slipping about 2 centimeters at the surface.

cards.title: A fault that slides the opposite way
cards.text: Unlike most other faults in California, the Garlock Fault slips left-laterally. It is believed to have developed to take up the strain between the stretching crust of the Great Basin and the faulting of the Mojave Desert crust. Geologists have described it as a fault that accommodates stretching in the Basin and Range country to the north, relative to the steadier Mojave block to the south.

cards.title: The lake that filled the valley
cards.text: Today Indian Wells Valley holds dry playas, but during the Pleistocene it held perennial lakes. Radiocarbon dates show an ancestral China Lake existed between about 14,690 and 32,220 years ago. Outflow from Owens Lake into the valley increased during that time, creating a sizeable lake. Shallow sediments under the China Lake playa today appear to be late Pleistocene in age, probably because wind scour removed younger sediments.

cards.title: A basin with no way out
cards.text: Indian Wells Valley has entirely internal surface drainage, so no stream carries its water out of the valley. A steep fault scarp runs along the base of the Sierra Nevada, and broad alluvial fans spread from the mouths of its canyons. The fans have coalesced into alluvial plains several miles wide that slope toward the playas along the east side of the valley. China Lake, the largest and lowest playa, is at an altitude of 2,152 feet.

cards.title: Fossil Falls, carved by the Owens River
cards.text: At Fossil Falls, in the Coso Range near Little Lake, the Owens River was forced to divert over a basalt flow, polishing and reshaping the rock into unusual shapes. The lava flows occurred between 400,000 and 10,000 years ago. The erosion came from the youngest glacial runoff, called the Tioga, from the Sierra Nevada about 20,000 to 10,000 years ago. Native Americans camped near the falls and chipped obsidian from the Coso Mountains to make tools. The Bureau of Land Management protects Fossil Falls as an Area of Critical Environmental Concern.

cards.title: The wells that named the valley
cards.text: Indian Wells Valley is named for Indian Wells, a set of springs on its western border. The old stage route from Mojave to Keeler runs along the western border of the valley, past those springs. The Los Angeles Aqueduct, which carries water from the Owens Valley to Los Angeles, has been cut into the escarpment of the Sierra Nevada from Little Lake to Indian Wells.

cards.title: Where the lake once spilled over
cards.text: A narrow gorge southeast of China Lake once afforded the lowest exit for surface drainage from Indian Wells Valley. It is now filled with windblown sand and is part of the Salt Wells Valley drainage, and the divide on it has a surface altitude of 2,190 feet. A granite ridge at an altitude of about 2,400 feet marks the apparent site of rapids of another outlet, used when the level of a perennial lake was above 2,400 feet.

cards.title: Rain from October to March, wind all year
cards.text: Average rainfall on the valley ranges from about 6 inches to less than 4 inches. Most of the precipitation on the valley floor comes between October and March, and the rest of the year rain falls infrequently, as summer thundershowers. Relatively high wind velocities are common in the valley, and the prevailing winds blow from the southwest. Strong northerly winds are also recorded occasionally.

cards.title: A river that follows a fault
cards.text: The Kern Canyon Fault runs the length of the Kern River canyon, from the river's headwaters down to the Walker Basin. The fault was reactivated some 10 million years ago, and the Kern River modified its course to its present drainage path out of the foothills. The fault is geologically active. In the Sierra Nevada, the river sits in a classic V-shaped canyon as it erodes toward base level.

cards.title: The killer Kern
cards.text: The Kern River is well known for its danger and is sometimes called the Killer Kern. Every spring, snowmelt from the Sierra transformed the river into a swollen fury. In 1966, 598,400 gallons of water per second raged over the Isabella Dam spillway, and Bakersfield was not flooded. The river is also a popular destination for whitewater rafting and kayaking.

cards.title: From Mount Whitney to the valley
cards.text: The Kern River is approximately 165 miles long. It is fed by snowmelt near Mount Whitney and begins in the Sierra Nevada in Sequoia National Park. In Lake Isabella, the Kern is joined by its largest tributary, the 95-mile South Fork. Below Lake Isabella, the river feeds several hydroelectric plants.

cards.title: Basins, ranges, and dry lakes
cards.text: The Mojave Desert has basin and range topography, a series of parallel mountain ranges and valleys. Water that collects in the basins generally evaporates. That leaves dried lake beds called playas, with large volumes of salt.

cards.title: The tree that marks the desert
cards.text: The Joshua tree is an indicator species of the Mojave Desert, and it is endemic to it. In Joshua Tree National Park, the western half is Mojave Desert and has thousands of Joshua trees. The eastern half, in the Colorado Desert, has ocotillo and smoketree instead.

cards.title: The King Clone creosote ring
cards.text: A ring of creosote bushes in the Mojave Desert near Lucerne Valley is estimated to be 11,700 years old. The ring is a single clonal colony, one plant that has spread outward over thousands of years. It was identified and dated by Frank Vasek, a professor at the University of California, Riverside.

cards.title: A desert in the rain shadow
cards.text: The Mojave Desert is found primarily in southeastern California and southwestern Nevada. It lies in the rain shadow of the southern Sierra Nevada and the Transverse Ranges. Storms drop their rain and snow mostly on the mountains, which leaves the slopes on the far side drier. In the Mojave part of Joshua Tree National Park, about 3 to 5 inches of rain fall in a year, mostly in winter.

cards.title: The Adelaida District
cards.text: Chimney Rock Road and Nacimiento Lake Drive form part of the boundary of the Adelaida District, the wine district in the far western part of the Paso Robles region. The district climbs the Santa Lucia Range, from foothills at about 900 feet to high slopes at about 2,200 feet. Here the ocean's influence is modest, with light sea breezes and little fog. Its soils are thin, lying on bedrock, and much of it is calcareous, meaning rich in lime.

cards.title: Highway 46 as a wine line
cards.text: East of Paso Robles, stretches of Highway 46 form the line between two wine districts, the Paso Robles Estrella District and the Paso Robles Geneseo District. They are two of eleven districts drawn inside the larger Paso Robles wine region in 2014. The Estrella District is the rolling plain of the Estrella River valley, while the Geneseo District is hills pushed up along a fault through old river terraces. A wine labeled with one of the district names must also say Paso Robles, unless the district's name already includes it.

cards.title: Hot days, cold nights
cards.text: Summer days in Paso Robles are hot: at the airport, the average high in July is about 93 degrees. But the nights are much cooler, and across the wine region the gap between a growing-season day's high and that night's low runs from 20 to 50 degrees. The climate is set by the sea in the west and turns more continental, less touched by the ocean, toward the east.

cards.title: A wine region since 1983
cards.text: The vineyards around Paso Robles grow inside the Paso Robles wine region, which the federal government recognized as an official American Viticultural Area in 1983. Commercial winemaking here began in the 1880s, with the Ascension Winery, later called York Mountain Winery. The Paso Robles wine festival began the same year the region was recognized, and growth in the 1990s made wine tourism part of the local economy.

cards.title: A stack of rock plates
cards.text: The Rand Mountains are built on a thrust fault that stacks one body of rock on another. Above the Rand thrust lie quartz monzonite and gneiss, and below it lies a rock called Rand Schist. The southwestern part of that fault was later reused as a low-angle normal fault. In the middle Miocene, the Rand Detachment Fault helped stretch the northwest Mojave Desert.

cards.title: The great earthquake of 1857
cards.text: The ground here at Cholame was torn open by the Fort Tejon earthquake of 1857, one of the largest earthquakes in California's recorded history. It was about magnitude 7.9, it began not far from here, and the break ran southeast along the fault for some 160 miles. In places the two sides of the fault slipped about 30 feet. Trenches dug beside Highway 46 here show the 1857 break in the layers of soil, along with signs of the Great Flood of 1861.

cards.title: Where the fault locks
cards.text: The San Andreas Fault, which runs within a mile of Cholame, marks about 800 miles of the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates. Cholame sits near a turning point in how the fault behaves. Farther northwest, beyond a transition zone, the fault creeps, its two sides slipping past each other slowly, with many small earthquakes but no large ones. South of Cholame the fault appears to be locked, and that is the stretch where large earthquakes, including the great one of 1857, have struck.

cards.title: The fault at Parkfield
cards.text: The San Andreas Fault runs northwest from here at Cholame to Parkfield, {distance} from here, where the fault breaks with unusual regularity. Earthquakes of about magnitude 6 struck that stretch in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934 and 1966, roughly one every 22 years. Scientists expected the next one between 1988 and 1993, and set up instruments there to catch it. It did not come until September 28, 2004. Parkfield's motto is: Be here when it happens.

cards.title: Digging into the fault
cards.text: Highway 46 crosses the San Andreas Fault here at Cholame. In 1966 an earthquake broke the ground along the fault and shifted the highway's pavement by about 4 inches. Before building a new bridge here, Caltrans geologists dug two trenches, each 300 feet long, across the fault, to see whether the bridge could avoid its active strands. They called the dig the James Dean Paleoseismic Site, for the actor who died in a crash nearby in 1955.

cards.title: Granite on the move
cards.text: The Santa Lucia Range, the mountains around Adelaida, has a core of granite on a slab of the earth's crust that lies west of the San Andreas Fault and is still moving northwest along it. Over roughly the past 30 million years, slivers of that granite have been carried northwest from where it formed. Where that was is still debated: it has been matched to the Sierra Nevada, but some geologists say it looks more like granite from the Mojave Desert.

cards.title: Wet side, dry side
cards.text: The Santa Lucia Range, the mountains around Adelaida, catches the Pacific's moisture on its western slopes and leaves the valley to its east, where Paso Robles lies, much drier. Here on the drier east side, the slopes carry chaparral and open woods of pine and oak, while the ocean side of the range grows redwoods and Douglas fir. At the Paso Robles airport, only about 12 inches of rain falls in an average year. In the Adelaida wine district, up on the range's slopes, it is about 25 inches.

cards.title: Named for Saint Lucy
cards.text: The mountains west of Paso Robles, where Adelaida sits, are the Santa Lucia Range, a rugged range that runs along the central California coast. The Spanish explorer Sebastián Vizcaíno named them in 1602, sailing past around Saint Lucy's feast day in December. For early Spanish explorers, the range was a barrier along the coast. In 1769 the Spanish Portolá expedition, traveling overland, found the coast impassable and had to turn inland through the mountains.

cards.title: Layers that record the climate
cards.text: Beneath the dry bed of Searles Lake, layers of salt and mud record how the lake rose and fell. Over the past 150,000 years, the lake had about thirty major swings in level. The swings match the advances and retreats of glaciers in the Sierra Nevada. One dating study suggests the lake dried out at most twice in the last 600,000 years, around 290,000 years ago and again from about 10,000 years ago to the present.

cards.title: When Searles Lake spilled over
cards.text: At times in the Ice Age, Searles Lake filled until it overflowed. Its overflow ran into Panamint Valley, which held a lake about 60 miles long. Dating of the lake sediments shows that overflow from Searles to Panamint happened in four separate windows of time. Lake Panamint itself overflowed into Death Valley at times, through Wingate Pass.

cards.title: The animals that had this floor first
cards.text: The San Joaquin kit fox, the blunt-nosed leopard lizard and three kinds of kangaroo rat live in this valley, and every one of them is listed as endangered. The natural land they depend on is generally down to less than five percent of what was once here, in scattered fragments. One federal recovery plan covers 34 species of plants and animals in this valley.

cards.title: The floor of the valley is sinking
cards.text: The ground under this valley has been settling since about 1920, when farmers began leaning on groundwater. By 1970 about half the San Joaquin Valley, some 5,200 square miles, had dropped more than a foot, and in places the drop has reached 28 feet. Between 2015 and 2016, satellite measurements found parts of the valley going down as fast as two feet a year. The sinking has cut the carrying capacity of the California Aqueduct and other canals, and the repairs are expensive.

cards.title: The lake that used to be here
cards.text: This end of the San Joaquin Valley is a closed basin, and the rivers running into it never reach the sea. Five rivers, the Kern among them, fed Tulare Lake, {distance} from here, once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi. By 1899 it was dry but for marshes and the occasional flood. The storms of early 2023 brought back more than 114,000 acres of it.

cards.title: Granite from six miles down
cards.text: Most of the southern half of the Sierra Nevada is made of granite and other plutonic rocks of Mesozoic age. That granite was emplaced about 6 miles below the surface. The Sierra Nevada batholith pushed into strongly deformed but weakly metamorphosed sedimentary and volcanic rocks of Paleozoic and early Mesozoic age, known as the framework rocks.

cards.title: From sagebrush to Jeffrey pine
cards.text: The Owens Peak Wilderness area is steep and rugged, with elevations ranging from about 4,500 feet to 8,453 feet at the summit of Owens Peak. Sagebrush and mountain mahogany grow on the lower slopes. The middle elevations have digger pine, live oak, ceanothus, manzanita, and chinquapin. Higher country is covered by Jeffrey pine, incense cedar, black oak, and ceanothus, with rare sugar pine on the north side of Lamont Peak.

cards.title: Owens Peak
cards.text: Owens Peak rises to about 8,450 feet in the southern Sierra Nevada, near the center of the Owens Peak Wilderness. It stands about 12 miles west-northwest of Inyokern. It is named for Richard Owens, an Ohio-born explorer who accompanied John C. Frémont on his third expedition to California in 1845 and 1846.

cards.title: Three generations of granite west of Owens Peak
cards.text: The granite of the Sierra Nevada batholith at Rockhouse Basin, 15 miles west of Owens Peak, comes from at least three major periods of intrusion. Most of that area is Cretaceous granite and granodiorite that is pale and shows no foliation. An older, darker set of granitic rocks is Jurassic or Cretaceous, and the oldest intrusive rocks are probably Jurassic or Triassic. The granite intrudes older quartz-mica schist, quartzite, and marble, with zones of calc-silicate hornfels where marble meets granite.

cards.title: A tilted block with a dry east side
cards.text: The Sierra Nevada is a huge block of the earth's crust that has been sharply uplifted and exposed on the east along the Sierra Nevada fault system and tilted westward. Rocks west of the Sierra fault moved up to create the modern mountains, while those to the east moved down to form a valley. The range forms a barrier to storms from the Pacific and creates a rain shadow east of the crest. The shallow western slope has pine forests and alpine lakes, while the steep eastern slope is barren and dry.

cards.title: Rock from deep underground
cards.text: In the Tehachapi Mountains, rock that formed 25 to 30 kilometers below the surface now lies exposed. These are Cretaceous gneisses from deep within the Sierra Nevada batholith. Seismic profiles show that the batholith rocks dip northward as a tilted slab beneath the southern end of the San Joaquin Basin.

cards.title: The pass everyone used before this one
cards.text: Until the railroad was pushed through Tehachapi Pass in 1876, the way over these mountains was not this pass but Oak Creek Pass, {distance} from here. Father Francisco Garces used it in 1776 to get back to the Mojave after exploring the San Joaquin Valley, and Fremont came through it in 1844.

cards.title: The wind through the pass
cards.text: Tehachapi Pass acts as a venturi for air moving between the ocean and the desert, which increases wind speed. Wind development in the pass began in the early 1980s. The first turbines installed there were American-made and proved troublesome, so the developer turned to Danish machines.

cards.title: A salamander with no lungs
cards.text: The Tehachapi slender salamander lives only in California, in isolated areas of the Piute and Tehachapi Mountains in Kern County. It is about 3 inches long and dark brown, with coppery red and silver speckles. It has no lungs and breathes through its skin, which it must keep moist. It lives in damp leaf litter and comes out during high humidity or rain.

cards.title: The range between valley and desert
cards.text: The Tehachapi Mountains form a range about 40 miles long in southern Kern County and northwestern Los Angeles County. They form part of the boundary between the San Joaquin Valley and the Mojave Desert. Oak woodland, oak savanna, and chaparral grow on the slopes, with mixed evergreen forest at higher elevations. Mountain lions, black bears, and mule deer live in the range.

cards.title: The White Wolf Fault
cards.text: Where the Tehachapi Mountains drop away to the San Joaquin Valley, they meet the White Wolf Fault, which broke in 1952 in a magnitude 7.3 earthquake. It is a reverse fault, meaning one side rode up over the other, with some sideways movement as well. That earthquake was the largest in southern California since 1857, and it killed twelve people.

cards.title: Josh Brolin grew up out here
cards.text: Josh Brolin, who played Thanos in the Avengers films and starred in No Country for Old Men, was raised on a ranch in the Adelaida area west of Paso Robles. He went to elementary and middle school in Templeton, and moved to the Santa Barbara area at about the age of eleven. His first big film role was Brandon Walsh in The Goonies, in 1985. He was later nominated for an Academy Award for his part in the film Milk.

cards.title: Buck Owens made his career here
cards.text: Buck Owens, who co-hosted the television show Hee Haw from 1969 to 1986, led the Buckaroos, a band with 21 number one hits on the Billboard country chart. Born in Texas in 1929, he first saw Bakersfield in the late 1940s while driving a truck through the San Joaquin Valley, and he settled here in 1951. The style he pioneered is named for his adopted home town: the Bakersfield sound. He died at his ranch just north of Bakersfield in 2006.

cards.title: A Chief Justice grew up in Bakersfield
cards.text: Earl Warren, Chief Justice of the United States from 1953 to 1969, grew up in Bakersfield. Born in Los Angeles in 1891, he moved here with his family in 1896. Warren graduated from Kern County High School in 1908, and he went on to become the first Governor of California elected to three consecutive terms. As Chief Justice he helped arrange a unanimous decision in Brown versus Board of Education in 1954, and he led the commission that investigated the assassination of President Kennedy.

cards.title: Korn started in Bakersfield
cards.text: Jonathan Davis, the singer of the band Korn, was born in Bakersfield on January 18, 1971 and raised here. At the age of 16 he found work as a coroner's assistant, and later apprenticed at the Kern County Coroner's Department. He co-founded Korn in Bakersfield in 1993. He also plays the Highland bagpipe, which first turned up on a Korn song called Shoots and Ladders.

cards.title: The man who drew Tinker Bell
cards.text: Marc Davis, the Disney animator who drew Tinker Bell, Cruella de Vil and Maleficent, was born in Bakersfield on March 30, 1913. He was one of Disney's Nine Old Men, the core animators of the studio's animated films, and he also drew Aurora in Sleeping Beauty. Later he moved on to designing rides for Disneyland, among them Pirates of the Caribbean and the Haunted Mansion. Walt Disney called him his Renaissance man.

cards.title: Merle Haggard was born in a boxcar
cards.text: Merle Haggard, who had 38 number one hits on the country charts, was born on April 6, 1937 in Oildale, near Bakersfield. His parents had come to California in 1934 after their farm in Oklahoma burned down, and his father remodeled a railroad boxcar in Oildale into the house where Merle was born. The boxcar was moved to the Kern County Museum in 2015, {distance} from here.

elsewhere.name: the Kern County Museum in Bakersfield

cards.title: Four Indianapolis 500 wins out of Bakersfield
cards.text: Rick Mears, one of only four men to win the Indianapolis 500 four times, was raised in Bakersfield. He was born in Wichita, Kansas, and started out in off-road racing. He won at Indianapolis in 1979, 1984, 1988 and 1991, and he still holds the record there for pole positions, with six. He was also a three-time Indycar champion, in 1979, 1981 and 1982.

cards.title: Antelope Grade
cards.text: Antelope Grade is the western side of Polonio Pass, a low pass where the Temblor Range to the south meets the Diablo Range to the north. The hills on either side are mostly gently rolling grassland. Highway 46 crosses here at the southern end of the Diablo Range, on one of the routes linking the Central Valley to the coast. In 1912 an ethnographer described Cholame as sitting at the easiest pass to the Tulare Lakes. Voters approved this highway, linking the valley with the coast, in a state bond issue in 1916, and it was fully paved by December 1930.

cards.title: Buck Owens built a palace for it
cards.text: In 1996 Buck Owens opened the Crystal Palace in Bakersfield, a nightclub for country performers and a museum of his own career under one roof. The building on Buck Owens Boulevard was built in a Western Revival style, made to look like the Old West, and the museum filled display cases around the ground floor. After nearly thirty years, it closed in August 2025.

cards.title: Why it had to be a Telecaster
cards.text: The guitar behind the Bakersfield sound was the Fender Telecaster, and Buck Owens bought his first one in 1951, the year it came out. Its jangly treble could cut through the racket of booming bass drums. Nashville was going the other way at the time, toward warmer hollow-body guitars and syrupy strings.

cards.title: A city with a sound named after it
cards.text: Bakersfield has a sound named after it: a hard, electric guitar driven kind of country music that became one of the most popular country styles of the 1960s. It came together in honky-tonk bars here such as The Blackboard, and on local television stations in Bakersfield and around California. The signature was twin Fender Telecasters, picked rather than strummed, a big drum beat and fiddle, with an occasional pedal steel solo. It was a reaction against the slickly produced, orchestra-laden Nashville sound, and Nashville's big radio station did not reach California anyway.

cards.title: The canal running beside the road
cards.text: The big concrete canal running beside Interstate 5 through this part of the valley is the California Aqueduct, and the town of Lost Hills stands on its east bank. It is the main work of the California State Water Project, and it serves about 35 million people and 5.7 million acres of farmland. A typical stretch is 40 feet across at the bottom, with the water about 30 feet deep. Altogether it runs 444 miles.

cards.title: Water pushed over a mountain range
cards.text: The concrete canal running down this side of the valley is the California Aqueduct, and it has a mountain range to get over. At the Edmonston Pumping Plant, {distance} from here, it is lifted 1,926 feet to cross the Tehachapi Mountains. Fourteen pumps of 80,000 horsepower each do the lifting, and the plant can draw 787 megawatts down a power line of its own.

cards.title: Where Cesar Chavez lived and is buried
cards.text: Cesar Chavez and his wife Helen moved into a small house here in 1971 and raised their younger children in it. From this place the United Farm Workers ran a national lettuce boycott and pushed through the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975. Chavez died in his sleep in April 1993, and Helen buried him here in what is now the memorial garden.

cards.title: A national monument in a village of a few hundred
cards.text: The United Farm Workers headquarters outside Keene has a second name, Nuestra Señora Reina de la Paz, which means Our Lady Queen of Peace. On the 8th of October, 2012, President Obama made it a national monument by proclamation, the 398th unit of the National Park System. The National Park Service runs it together with the National Chavez Center, and the 116-acre site holds a visitor center and the garden where Chavez is buried.

cards.title: A sanatorium before it was a union headquarters
cards.text: The farm workers' headquarters here was a tuberculosis hospital first. Kern County opened a rock quarry on the site in 1913, and a few years later the state's tuberculosis bureau chose the property for a sanatorium called Stony Brook Retreat, which took patients from the 1930s until it closed in 1967. In 1970 the United Farm Workers heard that the 187-acre property was going to public auction, and that year it was turned over to Cesar Chavez and the farm worker movement. The old sanatorium officially became the union's headquarters in January 1972.

cards.title: The Estrella Adobe Church
cards.text: The Estrella Adobe Church, on Airport Road north of Highway 46, was the first Protestant church built in northern San Luis Obispo County. Settlers on the Estrella Plains built it in 1879, making the adobe bricks on the site and hauling lumber over the mountains. As the congregations moved on to churches of their own, it fell out of use and crumbled into ruins. Young men from a boys' school made thousands of new adobe bricks to rebuild it, and it was rededicated in 1952.

cards.title: James Dean's last drive
cards.text: Near the junction of Highways 46 and 41, just east of Cholame, the actor James Dean was killed in a crash on September 30, 1955. He was 24, and was driving his new Porsche Spyder to a sports car race in Salinas. Coming west down the long Antelope Grade, he met a Ford turning left across his path onto Highway 41, and the two cars collided almost head-on. Dean was pronounced dead on arrival at the hospital, and his passenger, a Porsche mechanic who was thrown from the car, survived.

cards.title: A memorial from Kobe
cards.text: In Cholame, in front of the old post office, stands a stainless steel memorial to James Dean, built around a tree of heaven. It was put up in 1977 by Seita Ohnishi, a retired businessman from Kobe, Japan, who admired Dean's film East of Eden. The sculpture was designed in Japan, and Ohnishi chose this spot after examining the nearby crash site. Etched into it is one of Dean's favorite lines, from The Little Prince: what is essential is invisible to the eye.

cards.title: The Wye
cards.text: The meeting of Highways 46 and 41 here has been named the James Dean Memorial Junction since September 30, 2005, fifty years to the day after the actor died in a crash near the site. It was long known as the Wye, for its triangle shape, a layout built in 1958, after Dean's death, that had a higher than average collision rate. The old two-lane highway running west from here was called Blood Alley, for its many head-on collisions. In June 2025 a new overpass opened here, so drivers heading for Highway 41 no longer turn left across oncoming traffic.

cards.title: What is left of a drowned valley
cards.text: Of the natural land that once covered this valley floor, generally less than five percent is left, broken into scattered pieces. One of the surviving pieces is Kern National Wildlife Refuge, {distance} from here, about eleven thousand acres of desert upland, old riverside woodland and marsh. It sits on the southern edge of what was once the largest freshwater wetland in the western United States, Tulare Lake. It was set aside in November 1960 to give migratory birds, above all ducks and other water birds, somewhere to spend the winter.

cards.title: Dragon Lake
cards.text: Lake Nacimiento, northwest of Paso Robles, is a reservoir on the Nacimiento River, known locally as Dragon Lake for its shape. The lake lies in San Luis Obispo County, but the dam is owned and run by Monterey County's water agency. Its main job is to catch winter floods and let the water out slowly, so it can soak into the underground water that Salinas Valley farms depend on.

cards.title: Water for Paso Robles
cards.text: Since 2011 a pipeline has carried water from Lake Nacimiento to Paso Robles, Templeton, Atascadero and San Luis Obispo. San Luis Obispo County had secured its share of the lake's water back in 1959, two years after the dam was finished. The Nacimiento River floods readily, so in a wet winter the lake can fill fast from downpours in the Santa Lucia Range upstream. In droughts it can sit low for several years in a row.

cards.title: Rock made of microscopic shells
cards.text: The oil under this field is held in diatomite, a rock made of the silica skeletons of countless microscopic water plants. It is up to 70 percent empty space, light enough to float on water, and almost impermeable. There are an estimated 2.2 billion barrels of oil in the ground here, and only about five percent of it has come out. The only way to move it is to fracture the rock.

cards.title: They were drilling for water
cards.text: Highway 46 runs through the Lost Hills Oil Field, from east to west. The field was found by accident in July 1910, when two drillers named Martin and Dudley were sinking a water well. They hit oil at 530 feet down. Production peaked early: four million barrels came out of the ground in 1917 alone.

cards.title: The ground here is going down
cards.text: Taking the oil out from under this field has made the ground sink. The middle of the field has dropped as much as eight feet, and the field as a whole goes down about nine inches a year. Radar satellites watched parts of it fall more than an inch a month through 1995 and 1996.

cards.title: Six hundred thousand batteries at Monolith
cards.text: At the Monolith substation here, Southern California Edison switched on a battery in 2014 built out of 608,832 lithium-ion cells. It held 32 megawatt-hours and could deliver 8 megawatts, enough to run between 1,600 and 2,400 houses for four hours. When it was switched on it was the largest lithium-ion battery system running in North America, and it lasted eight years before it was shut down in 2022.

cards.title: Los Angeles built a cement plant up here
cards.text: The cement works at Monolith was built by the city of Los Angeles, to make cement for the aqueduct that brings its water down from the Owens Valley. The settlement was simply called Aqueduct at first, and its post office opened under that name in 1908. William Mulholland, the engineer behind the aqueduct, renamed the place Monolith in 1910 for the huge limestone deposit in the hill. In its first two and a half years the plant turned out 1,200,000 barrels of cement, and 900,000 of them went into the aqueduct.

cards.title: The plant is still at it, under its sixth owner
cards.text: The cement works beside the road here is still running, and still the reason Monolith exists. It belongs now to UNACEM, a Peruvian company that bought it from Martin Marietta in the autumn of 2023. That made UNACEM the sixth owner since the city of Los Angeles built the place more than a hundred and fifteen years ago.

cards.title: The company decided it did not want a town
cards.text: Monolith was once a real town, with as many as 350 residents living across the road from the cement plant. Investors bought the works in the early 1920s, gave it the name Monolith and started selling cement on the open market, and the company put up houses for families and a bunkhouse for single men. Then in the 1960s the company decided it did not want to own a town anymore, the store closed in 1971, and the remaining houses were pulled down over the next few years.

cards.title: The day downtown fell
cards.text: Downtown Paso Robles took the worst of the San Simeon earthquake, which struck at a quarter past eleven on the morning of December 22, 2003. The magnitude 6.5 quake was centered in the Santa Lucia Mountains near San Simeon, {distance} from here, and the break in the fault ran southeast toward Paso Robles. Two women were killed when the Acorn Building, an unreinforced masonry building from 1892, collapsed. Some old masonry buildings that had been strengthened against earthquakes came through standing. Afterward California passed Jenna's Bill, named for one of the women who died, requiring warning notices on old masonry buildings that have not been strengthened.

cards.title: The Hole From Hell
cards.text: The 2003 earthquake broke open a hot spring under the parking lot of the new Paso Robles City Hall and library. Crews at first took the rotten-egg smell for a broken sewer line, until a local geophysicist, called in to look, saw the steam and knew it was a hot spring. A bathhouse had once stood on the spot, and its spring had been capped when it closed. Digging for the source left a huge pit, known around town as the Hole From Hell, and crews dug a trench to pipe the water to the Salinas River. It took until 2010 to fill the hole.

cards.title: Still working track
cards.text: The Tehachapi Loop is not a monument, it is working railroad. BNSF runs about 20 trains a day through it and Union Pacific about 16, which comes to an average of around 36 freight trains a day. The siding on the loop is called Walong, named for a Southern Pacific district roadmaster, W. A. Long.

cards.title: Three thousand men and a lot of blasting powder
cards.text: The loop in the track here was cut through solid and decomposed granite by about 3,000 Chinese workers between 1875 and 1876. They had little more than hand tools, picks, shovels, horse-drawn carts and blasting powder. The line over the mountains originally needed 18 tunnels and ten bridges, and the whole thing was finished in under two years, under the Southern Pacific engineer William Hood.

cards.title: A train that passes over itself
cards.text: To gain height here, the railroad goes round in a full circle and crosses over its own track. The circle is about 1,210 feet across, and a train climbing it gains 77 feet at a steady grade of around two percent. Any train longer than about 3,800 feet, roughly 56 boxcars, passes over itself going around.

cards.title: Turbines of several eras, side by side
cards.text: The turbines in Tehachapi Pass are not all of one age. Several generations of the technology stand here together, from early machines rated in kilowatts to modern ones producing up to three megawatts each. Wind development started in this pass in the early 1980s, and about 3,400 turbines stand here now.

cards.title: More than half the state's wind is here
cards.text: The turbines standing on both sides of Tehachapi Pass are a large share of California's wind power. The projects here and out in the Antelope Valley add up to 3,254 megawatts, out of 6,171 megawatts operating in the whole state. In 2024 California's wind farms generated about 7 percent of all the power made inside the state.

cards.title: The limit was the wire, not the wind
cards.text: For years what held back the wind farms in Tehachapi Pass was not wind but wire. A transmission project to fix that began in 2008 and was finished in 2016, with room for 4,500 megawatts. That opened the pass and the country around it to as much as 10,000 megawatts of wind.

cards.title: The man who kept the last elk
cards.text: Miller and Lux, the cattle company with its headquarters and store at Buttonwillow, owned about 1.4 million acres of land. When California's tule elk were thought to be extinct, Henry Miller sheltered the survivors in the wetlands around Buena Vista Lake, gave them 600 acres of open range and rewarded his men for reporting anyone who disturbed them. A count in 1895 found 28 of them left. The state bought 953 acres near Tupman for them in 1932, and the herd there is kept at about 30 to 35 animals, {distance} from here.

cards.title: A city planned for the desert
cards.text: California City dates to 1958, when developers bought 82,000 acres of desert to build a metropolis. The plan came from Nat Mendelsohn, a real estate developer and sociology professor, who wanted a community that would join the ranks of America's great cities. Streets were named after top universities and car makers, such as Stanford, Yale, Pontiac, and Cadillac. Vacant lots sold for 990 dollars. By 1962, only 175 homes had been built, and the grid of paved roads still has little construction.

cards.title: The third-largest city by area
cards.text: California City covers about 204 square miles, the third-largest land area of any city in California, behind San Diego and Los Angeles. Its plan included a central park with a 26-acre manmade lake and two golf courses. When it incorporated in 1965, it had 5,900 landowners but only 817 residents.

cards.title: From freeway to expressway
cards.text: Between 1963 and 1975, significant portions of US 6, now Highway 14, were moved to a freeway alignment. The last interchange near California City is California City Boulevard, and the road's character changes there. The former routing south of Mojave and the current routing to the north are both still known as Sierra Highway.

cards.title: The Fremont Valley
cards.text: The Fremont Valley stretches from the town of Mojave about 70 kilometers northeast to the foothills of the Lava Mountains and Summit Range. The Rand Mountains lie at its eastern edge, the southern Sierra Nevada form its western border, and the Tehachapi Mountains border it from the southwest. Koehn Dry Lake lies in the valley, along with the communities of California City and Cantil.

cards.title: The wilderness of the El Paso Mountains
cards.text: The El Paso Mountains Wilderness covers about 23,780 acres and was created in 1994. Its central feature is Black Mountain, an extinct volcano and the highest point in the range. Wildlife there includes raptors, the Mohave ground squirrel, and the desert tortoise. Joshua trees grow on the western side of the mountain.

cards.title: Last Chance Canyon
cards.text: Last Chance Canyon runs through the El Paso Mountains from Saltdale in the south to Black Mountain in the north. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on December 5, 1972, and is known as the Last Chance Archaeological District. The canyon includes pictographs, villages, rock shelters, mills, and quarries, along with gold mining camps. The canyon is open to hiking, camping, and four-wheel-drive vehicles in most parts.

cards.title: Rhinos and palms in the Miocene
cards.text: The rocks around Red Rock Canyon preserve fossils from the Miocene, between about 13.5 and 7.3 million years ago. They include horses, camels, and three kinds of rhinoceros, along with a shovel-tusker named Serbelodon burnhami. Fossil plants include oak, cypress, and a palm.

cards.title: Where the shuttle came home
cards.text: Edwards Air Force Base, which Highway 14 passes close to at Rosamond, was often one of the main landing strips for NASA's Space Shuttle. On April 14, 1981, the shuttle Columbia touched down on Rogers Dry Lake at Edwards, ending the first shuttle mission after more than two days in space. Astronauts John Young and Robert Crippen were aboard. Crowds of well over 200,000 people watched the landing.

cards.title: Soledad Mountain
cards.text: Soledad Mountain rises just south of Mojave, and gold was first found there in 1894, when prospectors chased the Queen Esther and other veins. In 1933, George Holmes struck the Silver Queen vein, which revived mining across the district and drew in investors from South Africa. The Golden Queen Mining Company was organized in 1935 to consolidate four of the mountain's mines. The mines produced more than 10 million dollars from 1894 to 1942, before a federal wartime order shut down gold mining. By 2016, the mountain had reopened as a modern open-pit, heap-leach mine.

cards.title: The Jawbone Siphon
cards.text: At Jawbone Canyon, the Los Angeles Aqueduct dips into the canyon and back out through a pipe 8,095 feet long, with an 850-foot drop. It is the largest of the pressurized tubes along the aqueduct, and its chief engineer, William Mulholland, called this section the Jawbone Siphon. The pipe uses the pressure developed on the downslope to force the water up the far side. It burst in freezing weather in 1988. Europeans who settled the canyon around 1860 named it Jawbone because its shape resembled a mandible.

cards.title: Named for an animal that is not an antelope
cards.text: The Antelope Valley is named for the pronghorns that roamed there. Pronghorns are not true antelopes, but they have long been mistaken for them because of their close physical similarities with the true antelope of Eurasia. Early settlers, hunters, and travelers recorded many sightings of pronghorns in the valley. Locally caught and butchered pronghorn meat was often sold to local hotels.

cards.title: The western tip of the Mojave
cards.text: The Antelope Valley covers about 2,200 square miles, mostly in northern Los Angeles County and the southeast corner of Kern County. It is bounded by the Garlock and San Andreas fault systems. Joshua trees, California scrub oak, creosote, and wildflowers, notably the California poppy, grow there. People in the valley depend mainly on pumping groundwater from the valley's aquifers and on importing water from the California Aqueduct.

cards.title: The Kiavah Wilderness at the pass
cards.text: Highway 178 crosses Walker Pass at the north boundary of the Kiavah Wilderness. The wilderness was created in 1994 by the California Desert Protection Act, and it takes in the Scodie Mountains. Pinyon pine, juniper, and Joshua trees grow there. The Pacific Crest Trail travels the length of the wilderness for 17 miles.

cards.title: Up Freeman Canyon
cards.text: By 1870, a good wagon road ran the entire distance from Gilroy to Cerro Gordo for travelers using the Walker Pass route. Today Highway 178 serves automobile traffic over the pass, up Freeman Canyon. In the 1870s and 1880s, a hideout of the outlaw Tiburcio Vásquez and Cleovaro Chavez was near the trail at the foot of the pass, on the desert side.

cards.title: The wilderness above the valley
cards.text: Owens Peak Wilderness, in the mountains west of the Indian Wells Valley, was designated by the California Desert Protection Act of 1994. It is a transition zone between the Great Basin, Mojave Desert, and Sierra Nevada ecoregions. Its canyons hold springs with extensive riparian vegetation, with cottonwood and oak trees in the canyons and valleys. The Pacific Crest Trail passes through the wilderness along the crest and western side.

cards.title: Why it's called Poison Canyon
cards.text: Salt Wells Canyon, commonly called Poison Canyon, lies on Highway 178 about 10 miles out of Ridgecrest. It earned the name because the small stream at its west end contains toxic levels of several minerals. Rocks in the canyon known as the Fish Head Rocks were originally called the Whale Heads. They were originally painted sometime in the late 1930s or early 1940s.

cards.title: Trona Road becomes Highway 178
cards.text: About 7.8 miles of Trona Road became part of the state highway system in 1947, with the addition of Legislative Route 212. That portion runs from Poison Canyon westward and is now part of State Route 178. Pinnacle Road, which meets the highway here, is the entrance to the Trona Pinnacles, five miles away.

cards.title: Canebrake Ecological Reserve
cards.text: Canebrake Ecological Reserve lies in the South Fork Valley, on the north side of Highway 178. Before the state acquired it in 1994, the property was a ranch established around 1872. Its habitat types include valley foothill riparian, blue oak and digger pine, and Joshua tree. Hundreds of bird species occur there, and the cottonwood-willow forest shelters the endangered southwestern willow flycatcher and the state-listed western yellow-billed cuckoo.

cards.title: Where the Pacific Crest Trail meets the highway
cards.text: Walker Pass Campground sits just off Highway 178, at the junction of the Owens Peak and Cache Peak segments of the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail. It has eleven walk-in sites for Pacific Crest Trail hikers and tent campers, plus two sites for car camping. Pinyon pines and a few Joshua trees grow there, but no drinking water is available at the site.

cards.title: When this was Route 6
cards.text: From 1937 until 1964, this road was part of US Route 6, which had been extended from Greeley, Colorado, to Long Beach, California, on June 21, 1937. South of Inyokern, US 6 continued on to Long Beach. On July 1, 1964, US 6 was truncated at Bishop, and the part from Inyokern to Los Angeles became State Route 14.

cards.title: The Garlock Fault
cards.text: Johannesburg is one of the communities closest to the Garlock Fault, which is about 250 kilometers, or 160 miles, long. The two sides of the fault slide past each other horizontally, in what geologists call left-lateral motion. The last significant surface ruptures are thought to have come about 1050 A.D. near Tehachapi and about 1500 A.D. near Johannesburg. No earthquake has produced surface rupture on the Garlock Fault in historic times, though a magnitude 5.7 earthquake occurred in 1992. The fault is named for the mining town of Garlock, founded in 1894 by Eugene Garlock and now a ghost town.

cards.title: Mercury in the creek
cards.text: On a ridge of the Santa Lucia Range near Adelaida lie the old Klau and Buena Vista mines, which mined and processed mercury ore from 1868 to 1970. Mercury washed off the old workings into Las Tablas Creek and on downstream into Lake Nacimiento. Crews hauled away contaminated material from a drainage channel in 2000, and in 2006 the federal government made the mines a Superfund cleanup site. Because of the mercury, the state warns anglers about eating some kinds of fish from the lake.

cards.title: The town that moved to Paso Robles
cards.text: Adelaida was once a busy mining town, kept going in the 1880s by two mercury mines, the Klau and the Buena Vista. It had a saloon, a dance hall and a general store, and its post office lasted from 1877 to 1936. Most of its businesses later moved to Paso Robles, even though the mines kept running until about 1970. What is left of old Adelaida is the cemetery and a 1917 schoolhouse on Chimney Rock Road, which stayed open until 1964.

cards.title: The aftershock that finished downtown
cards.text: The great earthquake of July 21, 1952 broke windows across Bakersfield, brought down plaster and damaged the county jail. Then on August 22 came the strongest aftershock, magnitude 5.8. Damage was especially heavy to brick buildings, and of 264 buildings that shock damaged, 90 had to be brought down completely. The city was still dealing with the unreinforced masonry left downtown well into the 1990s.

cards.title: Named after a field
cards.text: Bakersfield is named after one man's field. Thomas Baker, a lawyer and a former colonel in the Ohio militia, moved to the banks of the Kern River in 1863, and the place became known as Baker's Field, a stopover for travelers. By 1870 it was becoming the principal town in Kern County. The memorial to Baker at city hall carries his motto: time will justify a man who means to do right.

cards.title: A river with no water in it
cards.text: The Kern River made Bakersfield, and for thirty miles through the city its bed is dry. The river built a broad plain here that once spread out into vast wetlands and seasonal lakes. Most of the flow is now taken off into canals for farms in the southern San Joaquin Valley, and it supplies the city's own water as well.

cards.title: Three hours in July 1889
cards.text: On July 7, 1889, a fire burned for three hours and destroyed most of Bakersfield. It took 196 buildings, left 1,500 people homeless and killed one man. It seems to have started when gas fumes from a stove caught fire in a house near 20th Street and Chester Avenue, and there was not enough water pressure in the line to fight it. The town rebuilt larger and grander, and mostly in brick.

cards.title: Two billion barrels next door
cards.text: Bakersfield sits beside the Kern River Oil Field, {distance} from here. By the end of 2006 that field had produced close to two billion barrels of oil, and it had more than nine thousand active wells, with Chevron as the principal operator. Steam flooding has made it possible to get out much of the oil that was once thought too hard to recover.

cards.title: Where the Dust Bowl ended up
cards.text: Bakersfield, a town known mainly for agriculture and oil, was the destination for many Dust Bowl migrants and others from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and parts of the Midwest. A federal camp for them stood at Weedpatch, {distance} from here, with running water for showers, bathrooms and laundry rooms, and wooden platforms for tents. John Steinbeck put the Joad family there in The Grapes of Wrath, and dedicated the book to the camp's administrator, Tom Collins. Three buildings from the camp are still standing: the community hall, the post office and the library.

cards.title: Bena's depot is in a museum now
cards.text: Bena's railroad station was built here in 1885, and the depot is no longer on the spot. In 1961 the Southern Pacific and Santa Fe railroads gave it to Kern Pioneer Village at the Kern County Museum in Bakersfield, {distance} from here. Its restoration was finished in the summer of 2020.

elsewhere.name: the Kern County Museum in Bakersfield

cards.title: The one tree the town is named for
cards.text: Buttonwillow is named for a single buttonbush tree that stood as a landmark on an old trail across the valley. The tree was an ancient Yokuts meeting place, and later the spot where settlers held their stock rodeos. Miller and Lux, one of the largest landowners in California, put their headquarters and store here about 1885. The tree has been a California historical landmark since 1951.

cards.title: A road course out in the cotton
cards.text: Buttonwillow has a racetrack named after it, Buttonwillow Raceway Park, {distance} from here. It opened in 1995, and it is owned and run by the California Sports Car Club. The layout drivers use most is three miles long with 23 turns. Since 2004 it has held the Super Lap Battle, a time attack event where cars run against the clock.

cards.title: Allen's Camp becomes Caliente
cards.text: Caliente started out as Allen's Camp, named for Gabriel Allen, who in the 1870s kept a cabin and a stock pasture here. The railroad renamed the place Caliente when its construction reached this point in April 1875. Caliente is Spanish for hot, and the name was shortened from Agua Caliente, proposed for the hot springs in the area.

cards.title: The man Bealville is named for kept camels
cards.text: Caliente still sits on the railroad, where trains climb toward the Tehachapi summit eastbound or run down toward Bakersfield westbound. Bealville, {distance} from here on the same line, is named for Edward Fitzgerald Beale, who served in the United States Army and as Superintendent of Indian Affairs for California and Nevada. In 1857 President Buchanan sent Beale to survey a wagon road to the Colorado River, and the trip doubled as an experiment with camels imported from Tunis as pack animals. The camels could travel for days without water and carried much heavier loads than mules, but they scared horses and mules, and the Army declined to continue.

cards.title: The end of the track
cards.text: Caliente was the end of the railroad for about sixteen months in the 1870s, while crews cut a line up over Tehachapi Pass. A force of up to three thousand men, most of them Chinese, did the heavy work on the mountain above the town.

cards.title: The cloudburst of 1932
cards.text: On September 30, 1932, many inches of rain fell in twelve hours above Caliente, and trees, rocks, earth and debris came racing down the creeks. Two people died in Caliente when buildings in the lower part of the town were destroyed, and at least fifteen were killed in all. The railroad lost nine trestles and bridges and many miles of track, built almost on the edge of the streambed, between Tehachapi and Bena. One boxcar that fell in was washed a mile and a quarter downstream before it jammed against a trestle.

cards.title: Sixty buildings, twenty of them saloons
cards.text: While the railroad was being built, Caliente had roughly sixty buildings, twenty or more of them saloons. Stage lines and a freighting company ran through here too. The post office opened in 1875, closed in 1883 once the construction crews had gone, and opened again in 1890. The general store was remodeled in 1980 to house that post office, which is still in operation.

cards.title: A test track in the desert
cards.text: The Honda Proving Center of California, near Cantil, has a 7.5-mile oval track and a 5-mile winding road course. It was established in 1990 and used mainly to test Honda and Acura automobiles, though motorcycles are tested there too. Honda closed it in 2010 and moved testing to Marysville, Ohio, then announced in 2015 that it would renovate and expand it. The renovated center opened in May 2017.

cards.title: A stone cliff on the railroad
cards.text: Cantil is Spanish for stone cliff, and it was one of a series of C names chosen for this stretch of railroad, along with Cambio, Cinco, and Ceneda. It was founded as a station on the Nevada and California Railroad in 1908 or 1909, when the line was extended from Owens Lake to Mojave. The first post office opened in 1916.

cards.title: The day SpaceShipTwo broke apart
cards.text: On October 31, 2014, Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo crashed in the Mojave Desert near Cantil, killing one of its two pilots. The craft broke apart during its fourth rocket-powered test flight, and debris was strewn across a 5-mile track near Koehn Lake. The surviving pilot, Peter Siebold, was badly hurt but lived, because his seat was ejected as the craft broke apart and he used a parachute. Investigators found that the copilot, Michael Alsbury, unlocked the tail feathering system too early, at Mach 0.8 instead of Mach 1.4.

cards.title: The Acres
cards.text: China Lake Acres, which local residents call The Acres, had 1,757 people at the 2020 census. That was down from 1,876 in 2010. It first appeared as a census-designated place in the 2000 census. It covers about 5.2 square miles, nearly all of it land.

cards.title: The Jack Ranch
cards.text: The cattle country around Cholame is the Jack Ranch, owned by the Hearst Corporation since the 1960s and still a working cattle ranch. William Welles Hollister bought Rancho Cholame in 1867 and sold a half-interest to Robert Edgar Jack in 1869. Jack married Hollister's daughter, Nellie, and became a leading wool grower before switching to cattle. The ranch is named for the Jack family, and it was Howard Jack, the last rancher in the family, who sold it.

cards.title: A name that would not go away
cards.text: Cholame takes its name from a Salinan village, one of the villages tied to Mission San Miguel, {distance} from here. Writing in 1912, an ethnographer called Cholame the most persistent of native village names. The name is on record from 1804, and in 1844 it went to a Mexican land grant, Rancho Cholame. The creek, the valley and the hills around Cholame all carry the name too.

cards.title: The first American overland came through here
cards.text: About February 1, 1827, Jedediah Strong Smith, the first American to reach Mexican California overland, passed near this spot with a party of fur trappers. They had come up from San Gabriel Mission, heading north to a land reported to be teeming with plenty of beaver.

near.name: Point on the Jedediah Smith Trail, near Edison

cards.title: A town named after a power company
cards.text: Edison was called Wade until a power company turned up. The Edison Electric Company built a substation on the site in 1902, and when the Southern Pacific Railroad arrived at Wade in 1903 it changed the name to Edison.

cards.title: Oil pumps among the orchards
cards.text: Edison sits inside the boundaries of the Edison Oil Field, with working wells around the town. General Petroleum found the oil in July 1928, and the field peaked in 1953, when it produced over 6.6 million barrels in the year. By the end of 2008 it had given up 149 million barrels and still had 914 active wells, worked by about forty separate companies. Oil pumps and storage tanks stand among row crops and orchards across much of the field.

cards.title: Coyote Holes
cards.text: Freeman Junction began as a stagecoach stop run by Freeman S. Raymond, a forty-niner, at a place called Coyote Holes. The place had that name because coyotes visited the springs there in droves to quench their thirst. The station stood where the Walker Pass road, now California 178, met the road to Los Angeles, now California 14. Raymond kept the stop going, with a post office added after 1889 or 1890, until his death in August 1909.

cards.title: A junction of old trails
cards.text: A bedrock mortar site near the original spring suggests that Native Americans regularly camped at what is now Freeman Junction. Explorer Joseph R. Walker passed this junction of Indian trails in 1834, and forty-niner parties split here after escaping Death Valley, some going west and some south. California registered the site as a historical landmark in 1961. By 1978 the town had died and its remains were removed by passersby, and today nothing remains.

cards.title: The bandit at Coyote Holes
cards.text: On February 25, 1874, the outlaw Tiburcio Vásquez and his band robbed several freight wagon crews at Freeman Raymond's station, which was then called Coyote Holes. Vásquez preyed on stages and freighters traveling between the Kern River mines and Los Angeles.

cards.title: A runway for car commercials
cards.text: Inyokern Airport's long runways, a legacy of the Navy's wartime buildup, have made it a popular place to film car commercials. Ads shot there include most spots from Saab's Born from Jets campaign, as well as ads for Volkswagen and Volvo. Top Gun: Maverick used the airport's hangar for scenes of Tom Cruise working on a vintage aircraft.

cards.title: Harvey Field
cards.text: Inyokern's airfield was dedicated as Harvey Field on May 10, 1944, in honor of Navy Lieutenant Commander Warren Harvey, for his work on aviation ordnance and fighter tactics. The Navy closed Harvey Field in April 1946 and returned it to the county a year later.

cards.title: A railroad town on the county line
cards.text: Inyokern takes its name from its location near the border between Inyo and Kern Counties. It was a railroad town, established along the Southern Pacific's Lone Pine Branch, which has since been removed. That branch ran north from Mojave to Owenyo, a few miles north of Lone Pine, and was built around 1912 and used to help build the Los Angeles Aqueduct. Inyokern's first post office opened in 1910.
